rationale: Both sets are real strategic material, not launch-confetti. A is a little sharper and meaner on capital-allocation risk with "A $12.3B private fintech is spending on 50-country expansion without disclosing whether it makes money," while B is a little cleaner on beat architecture with "How Brex built card issuing and local-currency reimbursement in 50 countries." Neither wins decisively because both stay mostly grounded, demand the right proof, and refuse the obvious slop instead of dressing it up for a sad parade.
gaps_in_A: "The startup card war moves offshore: Brex bets 50 countries is the thing Ramp can't copy quickly" overreaches: the update says Brex competes with Ramp, not that Ramp cannot copy it quickly.
"multinational-payroll problem" is imprecise for a corporate-card and expense-management launch; payroll is adjacent, not the fact pattern supplied.

"distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer" is plausible color, but not in the update. It should have been framed as a hypothesis needing customer proof, not stated as scene-setting fact.
gaps_in_B: "Enterprise customers pushed Brex, the startup card company, to go global" leans on an old positioning label; the update says Brex serves venture-backed startups and tens of thousands of businesses, not that it is still chiefly a startup card company.
"opening a new front against Ramp and the banks" is fair as a rivalry frame, but still needs competitor capability checks before it becomes more than Brex-versus-Ramp seasoning.

"The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" assumes wires were the prior workaround. Good customer-story shape, but the wire detail must come from a named customer, not the model's imagination.
